newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds slip back amid selling on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds slip back amid selling on U.S. data.

text.p: Irish bonds slipped back slightly amid moderate selling on Friday in line with an international market retreat on stronger than expected U.S. inflation data, dealers said.
"The bias has been towards selling by both domestic and non-resident investors today," a dealer said. "The U.S. data confirmed the Fed's worst fears and was by no means market-friendly."

Higher than forecast core producer prices and retail sales for March together with a big upward revision to Feburary retail sales heightened fears of near-term interest rate hikes and spooked markets around the globe.

March PPI excluding food and energy showed a rise of of 0.4 percent against market forecasts of about 0.1 percent. March retail sales excluding autos rose 0.5 percent against market forecasts of about 0.1 percent.
Dealers said the figures could well push the Federal Reserve into taking anti-inflationary measures as early as May.
The FTSE 100 fell along with gilts on the news with analysts predicting a Dow loss of around 50 points.
However, price action on the Irish bonds market had not suffered as much as many other markets on the day, dealers said, capped by strong domestic CPI figures on Thursday.
"Benign CPI numbers and some recent convergence have helped limit the damage from the U.S. data today," a dealer said. "Also, peripheral markets seem to be holding up quite well."
On Friday the 10-year spread over bunds in afternoon trading was at 90 basis points, while the five-year pick-up was at 142 basis points - outperforming Germany by three basis points, dealers said.

By 1500 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down four pence from Thursday's close at 101.54 to yield 6.09 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 15 pence from the close at 107.75 to yield 6.84 percent.
